name: aria2
summary: A multi-protocol download utility whose engine schedules request groups, splits resources into independently transferable segments, and exposes optional JSON-RPC and XML-RPC control.

features.name: Request-group download scheduling
features.description: aria2 groups download requests into RequestGroup objects and drives them through a DownloadEngine loop. Groups can be reserved, activated, halted, and reported independently, allowing multiple downloads to share one engine lifecycle.
benefits: Makes download lifecycle and aggregate statistics explicit per request group
Allows several downloads to be coordinated by one event-driven engine
costs: Group reservation and halt state add scheduling transitions around individual transfers
Shared engine progress couples unrelated downloads through one event loop

features.name: Segmented resource transfer
features.description: aria2's SegmentMan allocates byte ranges to concurrent requests, tracks in-flight segments, and recognizes or cancels segments as requests complete. The same segment-management boundary is used by HTTP-style downloads and by piece-oriented protocols through their storage abstractions.
benefits: Uses parallel byte ranges when a resource and servers permit them
Keeps partial progress addressable for retry and continuation
costs: Range ownership and overlap handling complicate correctness and retry behavior
More simultaneous connections can increase server load and local coordination

features.name: Protocol-specific piece and integrity storage
features.description: aria2 keeps protocol-specific transfer commands above piece and file storage abstractions. BitTorrent messages update PieceStorage and piece hashes, while HTTP and Metalink commands use the same request-group and file allocation lifecycle without implying that all protocols share one wire protocol.
benefits: Separates protocol message handling from file and piece completion state
Supports integrity checks and partial files across different download protocols
costs: Protocol handlers must preserve shared storage invariants
Piece, file, and protocol completion states can diverge during failure recovery

features.name: RPC-controlled download engine
features.description: The source includes RPC request and method objects that address download groups, add downloads, query status, and mutate options. The manual documents JSON-RPC and XML-RPC servers as control interfaces separate from transfer execution.
benefits: Permits external controllers to inspect and change downloads
Separates command/control transport from the download engine's transfer work
costs: Remote control adds authentication, authorization, and lifecycle configuration concerns
Control requests observe asynchronous state rather than making transfers synchronous

mathematical_views.question: How do queued, active, halted, and completed download groups advance under the DownloadEngine loop?
assumptions: A request group is a stateful unit with one or more file and transfer requests
Engine iterations and command results are transition events
The view abstracts socket readiness and protocol-specific wire messages

mathematical_views.question: Which byte ranges are available, in flight, completed, or cancelled for a resource?
assumptions: A resource is represented by a finite byte interval or piece set
Segment ownership is an implementation state, not proof of wire-level parallelism
The view abstracts protocol-specific request and response encoding

mathematical_views.question: How do RPC methods and protocol commands reach request groups, segments, and piece storage?
assumptions: RPC methods and protocol commands are control vertices
Request groups, segment managers, and storage objects are state vertices
Edges describe implementation calls and ownership, not guaranteed completion

benefits: Explicit lifecycle and aggregate scheduling for downloads
costs: Shared scheduling state couples transfer progress to engine iteration

benefits: Parallel ranges and resumable partial progress
costs: Range ownership and retry coordination increase state complexity

benefits: Common completion and integrity boundaries across protocols
costs: Protocol handlers must maintain shared storage invariants

benefits: External inspection and control of asynchronous transfers
costs: Control-plane security and asynchronous observation become operational concerns
